chapter_theme: General songs (பொதுப்பாடல்கள்), not tied to a shrine: most confess the lure of courtesans and their eyes, a few turn to old age, the funeral and Death's servants, one sets ritual pomp aside for a union where 'you and I' fall away, and one thanks Murugan for the grace that made the poet sing the Thiruppugazh; the praise draws on Siva's and the goddess's epithets, Vishnu's avatars and the war with Sura.
structure_note: Courtesans and lovemaking: 1128, 1130, 1132, 1135, 1136, 1137, 1138, 1141. Age, death and the funeral: 1131, 1133, 1139, 1140. 1127 sets temple ritual beside non-dual release; 1129 is a song of gratitude rather than plea; 1134 asks for the teaching of knowledge. 1130 and 1133 give most of their praise to the goddess, Murugan's mother.

1127.reading: The poet asks not to be bewildered by the pomp of worship, invocations and mantras, palm-leaf texts, pillared halls, places where Veda and Agama are chanted and fuel burned in sacrifice, but to be called by Murugan himself, 'come', and given, regularly and without difference, the state where 'you' and 'I' cease, the siddhi of bliss and release into supreme bliss. The praise is a battle where Chamundi and the ghosts rejoice, Brahma cries out, the sky cracks, the mango tree is cut at the root and the seven seas are drunk, and Murugan calls the gods back to rule their heaven.
1127.nuance: The opening list (ஆராதனை ஆடம்பரம், ஆவாகன மாமந்திரம், வேதாகமம் ஓதும் தலம், எரிதாம் இந்தனம்) is ritual the poet does not want to be lost in (மருளாதே); against it stands நீ நான் அற வேறின்றி நிற்க, a non-dual union. Several compounds in the first half (சவாலம்பனத்து, வேதண்டமத்த) do not split securely, so the exact list is uncertain.

1128.reading: The poet describes courtesans whose eyes are like a vel steeped in poison, who surround men and will not let them go, name a price for their arts of pleasure, and stay only if they get a share of wealth, offering false friendship; he asks whether he must suffer the fear and misery of such clowning. The praise names Siva who burned Kama when Uma came near, Murugan dwelling among devotees, the vel that struck the mountain and the demons, and the lord who freed the gods from prison and imprisoned Brahma.
1128.nuance: விலைகூறி and பொருள் கூறாகப் பெறில் நிற்கவும் name the bargain outright: the women stay only for a share of the money. கூடா நட்பு, 'friendship that does not join', is a Kural phrase for false friendship; the women are also மட்டைகள், worthless husks.

1129.reading: A song of thanks: the poet says he will never forget that Murugan gave him unfailing wisdom and understanding of the books he studied, kept him from perishing in a passing life, carried him across the sea of desire, set him in the state beyond speech and mind, and made him, a base man, famous for singing the wondrous Thiruppugazh with honey in every direction, freeing him from the three impurities, the three qualities and bubble-like births. The praise names Siva who drew Meru as a bow with the serpent for string and Vishnu as arrow and burned the three cities, Devayanai daughter of Indra, and Murugan's sword that cut down Sura and his clan.
1129.nuance: The song names its own book: அற்புதத் திருப்புகழ் தேனூற ஓதி. The plea of other songs is here a list of graces already given (கொடுத்ததும், அளித்ததும் ... மறவேனே). வாசாமகோசரம், beyond word and mind, and மலத்ரயம், குணத்ரயம் are Saiva doctrinal terms. ஏடு ஏவு ராஜதத்தினைப் பணித்ததும் may refer to some royal command or honour; its sense is uncertain.

1130.reading: The poet describes courtesans with poisoned eyes who call a man in with sweet looks, show their breasts, rouse desire and bargain over the price, laugh from the street and snatch whatever wealth comes, and asks whether he, a rogue whose mind melts at their talk, must waste away. The praise is almost all to the goddess: speaker of the Veda, with crescent-moon locks, who kept dharma with two measures of grain, wearer of the tiger skin, rider of the bull, younger sister of Vishnu, whose great treasure Murugan is.
1130.nuance: விலைபேசி and வருபொருள் கண்டு ஏற்கவே பறிக்கும் name the trade. The goddess's epithets run in a string ending in -ச்சி (குலத்தி, பேச்சி, இடைச்சி, சடைச்சி ...). இருநாழி படிகொடு அறம் காத்த points to the story, told of Kanchi, of the goddess who kept the charities with two measures of grain; I offer it as a likely allusion.

1131.reading: The poet pictures death: troubles crowd round, the false hut of the body is laid out, kin and sons gather and lament with many words and then leave, and red-eyed Yama strikes and drags the life away; before that, he asks, may he be freed of his deeds and praise in ever-new words the victory of Murugan's vetchi-garlanded shoulders? The praise names Murugan as the one who taught his father, with crescent and Ganga in his red matted hair, the meaning of knowledge, and as god-emperor of Vishnu with his discus and Brahma the tall potter.
1131.nuance: The kin weep and then go (அவர் ஏக), a single beat that empties the house before Yama (சமன்) arrives. The plea is not for rescue but to praise (புகழ் செப்பப் பெறுவேனோ) before the end. அப்பர்க்கு அறிவொக்கப் பொருள் கற்பித்திடுவோனே is the story of Murugan teaching Siva, here without naming Om. குயவன், potter, for Brahma the maker is unusual.

1132.reading: The poet tells how at night Kama shoots his flower arrows and women's eyes, carp-like, deer-defeating, nectar and poison together, net young men's lives, and how, drinking their lips and embracing them, he sinks into the whirlpool of union; he asks for the good undying feet so that he does not drown. The praise names Vishnu who shot the arrow through Ravana's ten heads and twenty shoulders, Murugan as guru to Siva who pitied three in the walled cities, and the lord pleased by the songs of devotees who melt day and night.
1132.nuance: சுழி மிதுன வாவி, the eddying pool of coupling, makes union a drowning, so the remedy is feet that do not perish (அழியா மன் நல் பதங்கள்). தெளிமருவு காரணத்து அமர்ந்த may name a place or a cause; I cannot tell which.

1133.reading: The poet traces a life of unceasing sorrow driven by the burning belly, toil for food, the years passing, hair greying, the name 'old man', faltering steps and failing eyes, and asks whether he will perish without reaching the abode of the Dancer's raised foot. The praise is a litany of the goddess's names (Abhirami, Nili, Suli, Gauri, Mayi, Sivai, Ambikai, who burned the three cities and shares Siva's side), whose son Murugan is, Valli's bridegroom, lord praised by Hari, Hara, Brahma, Indra and the gods.
1133.nuance: நடன் குஞ்சித வீடு is release imagined as the lifted foot of Siva's dance; the song asks for it from the son, not the father. விடிவது என்று, 'when will it dawn', is the old man's question. Two lines are corrupt (see source issues).

1134.reading: The poet asks not to melt under the sway of young women whose sharp eyes are like Kama's battle, but to sink into the dust of Murugan's feet with their koothalam garland until the mind dissolves, and to receive the teaching of a knowledge beyond word and mind. The praise tells the story of Prahlada at length, the boy who answered his Brahmin teacher with Narayana's name and the man-lion who tore his father from the pillar, and names Vishnu as uncle and Siva as father.
1134.nuance: மனோலயம், the dissolving of mind, comes from immersion in the dust of the feet (பாததூளியின் முழுகி), and the plea ends in வாசாமகோசர ... ஞானோபதேசம். The Prahlada story is told in Prahlada's own words (இரணிய ரூபா நமோ, அரி கரி நாராயணா).

1135.reading: The poet describes lovemaking in frank detail, the swaying waist, ringing anklets, scattered jewels, scented flowers on the bed, and asks whether, after melting in a union said to equal Kama's own, he must wander the earth exhausted. The praise names Siva who burned the cities with a laugh, kicked Death, destroyed Kama and wore the sea's poison, and Vishnu who brought Duryodhana down in the Bharata war, with a battle in which jackals feast.
1135.nuance: மதராஜன் மருவிய கலவி தனக்கு ஒப்பாம் is the boast inside the confession: the pleasure is called equal to Kama's, and its end is weariness (களைத்து).

1136.reading: The poet tells how he praised women's eyes as vel, carp, sword, flower, Death's messenger, deer and poison, wandered deluded to the end, spoke deceit and became a materialist, and asks whether he will die without his service being fulfilled. The praise is a battle in which the sea cries out and Murugan drives off the demons with vel and sword, the lord of the peacock and son of Indra's fortune, worshipped by the Veda.
1136.nuance: லோகாயதனாகி: the poet names the materialist school as one of his falls, beside false speech (படிறு சொல்). The list of eye-comparisons (வேலோ சேலோ ... எமன்விடு தூதோ) is the opening's whole substance. The plea's lines (நாடாய் வீடாய் அடிமையும் ஈடேறாதே பணிதியில் மூழ்கா) do not split securely, and I read them only roughly.

1137.reading: The poet opens by naming Murugan as the peacock-rider born of peacock-like Uma and the child of six mothers, confesses that he never melted in devotion, is caught between his two deeds and is without understanding, and admits that though the pleasure of union with women is slight, he cannot, cannot give it up; he asks for release. The praise pictures Sura as a golden mountain, a sea, primeval darkness, Yama with trident and fiery eyes, the fire at the end of the age, a flesh-eating king challenging gods, Hari, Brahma and the seven worlds, and names Murugan as the king who threw the vel at him.
1137.nuance: சுகம் அற்பமாகினும் ... விடவோ இயலாது இயலாதே is a rare admission: the poet grants the pleasure is small and still cannot leave it. The demon's challenge is in his own voice (அறையோ அறையோ), and the cries of the worlds answer (முறையோ முறையோ). Two words are corrupt (see source issues).

1138.reading: The poet describes in detail a night with a woman, from bowing at her feet and her offered smile and betel to the bed, the loosened cloth, the nail marks, the babbling and the reddened eyes, and asks whether he must wear himself out in such union. The praise is a battle in which the demons of the sea lose their crowns, the mango tree is cut, the Krauncha hill is smashed, and the vel is worshipped by the short sage who loves the mountain, ending with the green peacock.
1138.nuance: The scene is told as a sequence (பணிந்திட்டு, இருத்தி, அணைமேல் வீழ்ந்து, உடுத்த பொற்றுகில் அகல ...) and the plea is one line at the end (நொந்தெய்த்திடலாமோ). பருப்பதப்ரிய குறுமுனி is Agastya, here a worshipper, not named as Murugan's pupil.

1139.reading: The poet asks that before Death comes saying women, sons, kin, life and clan are ended and his body of blood, water and bone is put on the fire, Murugan remove the grief of his anxious senses and his place among base men who rise by shouting down rivals with quarrelsome books, and give him a life of worshipping his feet with love. The praise names Siva who rides the bull with moon in his locks and deer and axe in his hands as the father who graced his younger son, and Murugan who split the mountain and came on the peacock.
1139.nuance: கலகக் கலை நூல் பல கொண்டு எதிர் கதறி ... வென்று உயர் கயவர் is a sharp picture of learning used to win debates, which the poet counts as baseness. Death is காலன், and the body is the hut grown from blood, water and bone (குடில்).

1140.reading: The poet pictures his funeral day, kin wailing, the town giving up hope, drums rising to the sky and many dropping rice into the dead man's mouth, and asks Murugan to come then with his six faces and twelve arms on the peacock, with Vedas sounding, gods raining flowers and his old devotees gathered, to rout Death's army and take him, a prattling dog-like servant. The praise names the victory where Kali and the ghosts feasted, Murugan's wandering in Valli's forest where he became a young tree, and his birth from the mother on Siva's side who bore him without bearing.
1140.nuance: The funeral is told with its rites (பறை, திமிலை, முழவு, அரிசி வாய்மீது), and the plea answers it with a procession of its own, Murugan's arrival. மறலி படை யமபுரமும் மீது ஓட வே பொருது makes the rescue a battle against Death. மாதா பெறா, the mother who bore without bearing, is Uma, since Murugan came from Siva's eyes.

1141.reading: The poet heaps abuse on courtesans as lustful, deceitful, shameless, drunk on liquor till their clothes slip, wicked sinners, goddesses of misfortune who bring poverty and false shapes of illusion, and asks for a state in which he is not tossed about in the pleasure of union. The praise names Siva who burned the flying cities with Vishnu as arrow and granted his feet to three who kept him in mind, and Murugan who cut the mango tree and joined the hunter girl in a grove where cuckoos and anril birds call.
1141.nuance: வறுமை தந்திடு பாழ் மூதேவிகள், 'ruinous Misfortune-goddesses who bring poverty', ties the women to loss of wealth, and பேய் நீராகிய உணவு to drink. The abuse is a list of plural nouns ending in -கள் with no verb until the plea.

links.note: Both put the faithless woman beside liquor and make her the mark of lost fortune: the Kural's women, drink and dice are the company of those Fortune has left; 1141 calls the drinking courtesans themselves மூதேவிகள், Misfortune, who bring poverty.

Both picture the wailing kin at the funeral. Tirumular's kin turn back at the edge of town and leave the dead man to the fire; 1140 lets the kin wail and asks that Murugan come at that moment with his devotees, so that the dead man is not left alone.
Both stage the deathbed, the kin who lament and leave, and Yama's coming. 1131 asks only to praise Murugan before the end; 1140 asks him to arrive at the funeral itself and fight Death's army.

source_issues: Song 1129: unflagged garble லொ முவர் (line 15), probably ஒரு மூவர், the three spared at Tripura; the same garble recurs in 1141 (வொ முவர், line 15).
Song 1133: corrupt மா஡ண (line 14), probably மாரீ, and ஓ ஧ட்மு (line 22, flagged), probably ஓடு மூ (பிரமாவோடு மூவகையர்).
Song 1137: corrupt தத஧முழ்கி (line 9, flagged), probably ததி மூழ்கி (மகோததி, the great sea); unflagged கொநல்மு (line 15), probably கொடு மூ (மூவிலைவேல், the trident).
